title: Colors of the year

segments.voice: Yesterday, bells: they call to prayer, toll for the dead, and ring out for joy. Your line was for whom it tolls. When a bell or a chime rang yesterday, who came to mind? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

In the back room of a church there's a cupboard full of cloth. Purple, folded on one shelf. White and gold on another. A bright red. And a tall stack of green. One week, someone takes the green cloth off the altar and the pulpit, folds it away, and hangs up purple. The minister's stole changes to match. Nobody makes an announcement. But someone who comes every week can glance at the front of the church and know, without a calendar, what time of year it is. Today: colors of the year.

Churches that keep the church calendar mark its seasons with colors, on the altar, the pulpit, and what the clergy wear. The customs vary from church to church, and Orthodox churches have color customs of their own, but a pattern you may meet runs like this. First, purple. It's the color of Advent, the weeks of waiting before Christmas, and of Lent, the weeks of turning back before Easter. Purple is a king's color, and the Gospels give it a hard edge: before the crucifixion, Mark says, the soldiers "clothed him with purple," and mocked him as a king. So some readers hear in purple both waiting for a king and sorrow over what was done to one. Some churches use blue in Advent instead. Next, white. Christmas, and Easter. At the empty tomb, Mark says the women "saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a long white garment." White for the feasts, for joy, for light. Then, red. Pentecost, when the Spirit came on the disciples: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." Red is fire. Some churches use it on the days that remember martyrs too. Last, green. It's the color of the long stretches between the big feasts, which some churches call ordinary time. Green is growth, plain and slow. Ecclesiastes gives the whole cupboard its reason: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." In these churches, the year isn't one long gray line. Time has colors.

Here's the practice: wear the season's color, or simply hold it. If you know where the church year is right now, find something in its color, a scarf, a shirt, a ribbon, a leaf. If you don't know, green will do: it's the color of the ordinary stretches of the year. Hold it, or look at it, and breathe. Let the color stand for the season you yourself are in: waiting, celebrating, on fire, or just growing slowly. If you pray, you can say the line from Ecclesiastes: to every thing there is a season. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: Colors of the year. Purple, white, red and green, set out in churches to mark the seasons of the church calendar, so the time of year can be seen.
Your line: time has colors. Today, choose one color for the season you're in right now, and notice it whenever it crosses your path. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and other churches that keep the church calendar change the colors of altar cloths and clergy vestments with the seasons, often purple for Advent and Lent, white for Christmas and Easter, red for Pentecost and green for ordinary time; Orthodox churches have their own color customs.

fork.setup: it's Pentecost Sunday, the day the church remembers the Spirit coming on the disciples. you're setting out the cloth for the altar. which color?
fork.reveal: red, for fire: "there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them."

original.note: Greek: purple, the cloth the soldiers put on Jesus in Mark 15:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: the colors at the front of a church are just decoration.
what it means: each color marks a season of the church year, so the time can be seen.
what a scholar hears: Mark 15:17, where soldiers clothe Jesus in purple to mock him as a king: a royal color worn in seasons of waiting and sorrow.
